issues.legal_issue: A financial creditor’s application to commence corporate insolvency resolution is not time-barred where the debtor acknowledged the subsisting debt in writing before the original limitation period expired and the application was filed within the renewed limitation period.
material_facts: The financial creditor applied to commence insolvency proceedings after more than three years had elapsed from the date the loan account was declared a non-performing asset.
Before the original limitation period expired, the debtor made a written proposal to settle its debt and its financial statements and balance sheets recorded the outstanding liability.
The creditor filed its application within three years of the relevant acknowledgment.
issues.conclusion: A written acknowledgment of the subsisting debt made before expiry of the original limitation period starts a fresh limitation period; the application was therefore not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code applies the Limitation Act, as far as may be, to insolvency proceedings; Article 137 provides a three-year limitation period from accrual of the right to apply. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a written acknowledgment of a present subsisting liability, signed by the debtor or an authorized agent before limitation expires, starts a fresh limitation period; it need not include a promise to pay. Acknowledgment may be established by a one-time settlement offer or by entries in balance sheets and financial statements. The Court relied on Sesh Nath Singh v. Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Cooperative Bank Ltd., Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India, Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal, Khan Bahadur Shapoor Fredoom Mazda v. Durga Prasad Chamaria, and the balance-sheet cases approved in Bishal Jaiswal. It distinguished Babulal Vardharji Gurjar v. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries and noted that Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstruction Company did not consider a one-time settlement proposal.

predicates.financial_creditor_insolvency_applicatio: A financial creditor applied to commence insolvency resolution proceedings against a debtor.
predicates.written_signed_acknowledgment_of_subsist: Before the original limitation period expired, the debtor or its authorized agent signed a writing acknowledging a subsisting debt, including through a settlement offer or financial statement.
predicates.application_within_three_years_of_acknow: The financial creditor filed the insolvency application within three years after the written acknowledgment.

issues.definition: When a financial creditor applies for insolvency resolution, a timely signed acknowledgment of a subsisting debt allows the application to proceed if it is filed within three years of that acknowledgment.

issues.legal_issue: An unpaid money judgment, decree, or recovery certificate gives a creditor a fresh cause of action to apply for corporate insolvency resolution.
material_facts: A tribunal entered a final money judgment and issued a recovery certificate in favour of the creditor.
The debtor did not pay the amount due under the judgment or recovery certificate.
The creditor applied to commence insolvency proceedings within three years of the judgment or recovery certificate.
issues.conclusion: An unpaid final money judgment or decree, or an unpaid recovery certificate, gives rise to a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application, which may be filed within three years of the judgment, decree, or certificate.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(6), 3(10), 3(11), 3(12), and 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, a claim may be reduced to judgment, a decree-holder is a creditor, and non-payment of a debt due and payable is a default. Section 238A applies the Limitation Act, and Article 137 supplies the three-year limitation period. The Court applied the principle recognized in Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. v. Rajhans Steel Ltd., which was relied on in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India, and held that a final adjudication or recovery certificate for unpaid money creates a fresh right to recover that amount through insolvency proceedings.

predicates.unpaid_final_money_judgment_or_recovery_: A court or tribunal entered a final money judgment or decree, or issued a recovery certificate, and the debtor left the amount due under it unpaid in whole or in part.
predicates.application_within_three_years_of_judgme: The financial creditor filed the insolvency application within three years after the final judgment, decree, or recovery certificate.

issues.definition: An unpaid final money judgment, decree, or recovery certificate permits a financial creditor to apply for insolvency resolution within three years of that adjudication or certificate.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor may amend pleadings and file additional documents in a financial creditor’s insolvency application before a final order, subject to the adjudicating authority’s discretion where delay is inordinate.
material_facts: The creditor sought permission to add a final recovery judgment, a recovery certificate, financial statements, and a settlement proposal to its insolvency application.
The additional material was filed while the application remained undecided and before it was admitted or dismissed.
The adjudicating authority considered the additional material and admitted the application; the request was not affected by inordinate delay.
issues.conclusion: There is no general bar to amending pleadings or filing additional documents before a final order on the application. The adjudicating authority may, depending on the circumstances, decline a request where there is inordinate delay.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7(2) to 7(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, read with the prescribed application form and rules, do not prohibit additional pleadings or documents or impose a deadline for filing them before a final order. The fourteen-day period for ascertaining default under Section 7(4) is directory, and the statutory scheme does not require dismissal merely because that period has passed. The Court distinguished Babulal Vardharji Gurjar v. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries, noting that the additional material here was filed before the application was finally decided and was not an impermissible late-stage improvement of the case.
